description: Heap allocators decomposed. The mechanisms inside malloc/jemalloc/tcmalloc/mimalloc: size classes, free lists, per-thread caches, central allocation paths, arena structures, fragmentation strategies, and the OS-level sbrk/mmap interaction. Allocator quality dominates application performance for malloc-heavy code.

sub_mechanisms.name: size_class_binning
sub_mechanisms.definition: Allocations are rounded up to one of N pre-defined size classes (e.g., 8, 16, 32, 48, ... bytes for small; 4 KB, 8 KB, 16 KB, ... for large).
sub_mechanisms.why: Eliminates fragmentation within the bin — all allocations of class S take exactly S bytes. Trade-off: rounding waste (typical ~15% overhead). Modern allocators (jemalloc) use ~50 size classes covering common sizes finely.

sub_mechanisms.name: free_list_per_size_class
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each size class has a free list of available blocks. Allocation: pop from list. Free: push back. O(1) for small allocations.
sub_mechanisms.why: LIFO ordering maximises temporal locality — the most-recently-freed block is the next one allocated, likely still in cache. Free lists are the workhorse of fast small-object allocation.

sub_mechanisms.name: per_thread_arena
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each thread has its own allocation arena: per-thread free lists, per-thread metadata. Avoids cross-thread locks for typical allocations.
sub_mechanisms.why: Contention is the enemy of scalability. Per-thread arenas eliminate the lock-acquisition cost on most paths. glibc malloc has 'arenas' but limited count; jemalloc and tcmalloc maintain truly per-thread arenas. Critical for highly-threaded workloads.

sub_mechanisms.name: central_allocation_path
sub_mechanisms.definition: When per-thread free list is empty, request a batch of blocks from a central (shared) pool. Batch size is typically 32-512 to amortise the lock cost.
sub_mechanisms.why: Threads need new memory periodically. Going to a central pool requires synchronisation; batching amortises that cost. The central pool is itself partitioned to reduce contention.

sub_mechanisms.name: slab_allocator
sub_mechanisms.definition: Pre-allocate large memory regions ('slabs') for one size class. Allocate sub-blocks from the slab using a bitmap or free list.
sub_mechanisms.why: Slab allocation eliminates per-allocation metadata for small objects. Bitmap or list within the slab tracks which sub-blocks are free. Common in kernel allocators (Linux's SLUB); also used by some user-space allocators.

sub_mechanisms.name: buddy_allocator
sub_mechanisms.definition: Manages power-of-2 sized blocks. To allocate size S, find the smallest free block of size >= S; if larger, split in half repeatedly until matching. Coalesce on free.
sub_mechanisms.why: Simple coalescing strategy. Free buddies merge back to form larger blocks, fighting fragmentation. Used in Linux kernel for page allocation. Internal fragmentation is worst when sizes are slightly over a power of 2.

sub_mechanisms.name: arena_split_small_medium_large
sub_mechanisms.definition: Modern allocators (jemalloc, tcmalloc) split allocations: small (<8 KB) use per-thread free lists; medium (8 KB-2 MB) use size-class slabs; large (>2 MB) directly mmap'd.
sub_mechanisms.why: Different size ranges have different overheads. Small allocations need to be fast; mmap-per-allocation would dominate. Large allocations need OS support for unmapping; size-class binning would waste TBs of memory. Three-tier split matches use cases.

sub_mechanisms.name: metadata_separation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Allocation metadata (size, prev/next pointers) lives separately from user data. Reduces touched cache lines on alloc/free.
sub_mechanisms.why: Storing metadata inline (glibc's classic header-prefixes-user-data) means free() must touch the metadata line. Separating them lets the user data stay cold during free. jemalloc's chunk-based metadata exemplifies this.

sub_mechanisms.name: fragmentation_external
sub_mechanisms.definition: Free memory exists but is split into too-small pieces to satisfy a larger allocation. Total free > requested size, but no single block large enough.
sub_mechanisms.why: Bane of long-running processes. Allocator design fights fragmentation via coalescing, compaction, size-class restriction. Long-running servers often grow over time despite stable allocation rates — fragmentation is usually the cause.

sub_mechanisms.name: fragmentation_internal
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each allocation gets more memory than requested (rounded up to size class). Sum of overheads is internal fragmentation.
sub_mechanisms.why: Trade-off with size class granularity. Fine size classes (many bins) reduce internal fragmentation but increase metadata. Modern allocators tune this balance — typical internal fragmentation: 10-25% overhead.

sub_mechanisms.name: mmap_for_large_allocations
sub_mechanisms.definition: Allocations >= mmap threshold (typically 128 KB-2 MB) directly call mmap to get a fresh virtual memory range. munmap on free returns memory to OS.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lets the OS reclaim large allocations cleanly. Without mmap, large blocks stay in the heap forever — even after free — because brk() can't shrink the heap below a high-water mark. mmap allocations return memory to the OS on free.

sub_mechanisms.name: decommit_unused_pages
sub_mechanisms.definition: Allocator may madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) on pages it isn't using, telling the OS to reclaim physical frames. Future access page-faults and zeroes the page.
sub_mechanisms.why: Holds virtual address space but returns physical memory. Useful for long-lived allocators with variable working sets. jemalloc does this aggressively; helps with long-running server memory pressure.

derivation_rules.name: per_thread_arenas_eliminate_lock_contention
if: each thread has its own arena
then: common-path allocations don't contend on locks
derivation_rules.why: Lock contention is per-operation latency that becomes per-thread serialisation. Per-thread arenas eliminate it for typical paths. jemalloc + tcmalloc both make this their core scaling strategy; glibc malloc's bottleneck on highly-threaded workloads comes from limited arena count.

derivation_rules.name: size_class_binning_trades_overhead_for_speed
if: allocations are routed to fixed size classes
then: allocation/free becomes O(1) at the cost of internal fragmentation
derivation_rules.why: Variable-size best-fit search is O(log N) at best. Size-class free lists give O(1). The wasted bytes per allocation (~15% typical) is the cost; the constant-time allocation is the benefit. Universal in modern allocators.

derivation_rules.name: small_alloc_fast_path_dominates
then: the small-alloc path determines overall allocator performance
derivation_rules.why: Typical workloads: ~95% of allocations are small. Allocator throughput is dominated by the small-alloc path's CPU + cache footprint. jemalloc/tcmalloc/mimalloc all optimise this path heavily.

derivation_rules.name: free_list_lifo_preserves_temporal_locality
if: the free list pops the most-recently-freed block first
derivation_rules.why: Freed memory's cache lines are still warm. LIFO pop returns a block whose lines are likely in L1. FIFO would return cold lines, missing on first access. Universal allocator optimisation.

derivation_rules.name: mmap_threshold_separates_short_long_lived
if: allocations above a threshold use mmap
then: large freed allocations return memory to OS instead of holding it
derivation_rules.why: Heap-based allocations grow but rarely shrink (high-water mark). Long-running processes with one-off large allocations would balloon. mmap'd allocations munmap on free, releasing the physical memory back to OS.
